vyr · measurement ledger · schema 3

The data

Every value recorded in ledger.db (SQLite), as flat sortable tables: the performance matrix cell by cell, every other recorded value one value per row, and one row per ledger entry. Nothing is summarised, ranked or coloured here. Regenerated from the file by ./dev.py track (scripts/ledger.py) and never hand-edited; to change a number, take a measurement.

52 lines in the ledger · 52 runs · 916 matrix cells (798 measured) · 1939 other recorded values · latest 97e18c2 perf(core): a persistent typed animation tree — mutate, don't re-parse (#55) · how each number is produced: docs/performance.md.

vyr vs LVGL — instructions per frame, × the LVGL anchor

The comparison the project exists to answer, on its own axis — a multiple, not an index. LVGL is the 1× baseline (the flat line); each vyr tier sits above it at its actual multiple and descends toward it as vyr is optimised. Render-only on both sides (#44/#45), so it is renderer against renderer. 1× would mean “as cheap as LVGL”; below 1× would mean cheaper.

Hover a line for the exact multiple at that commit. The same numbers are in the tables below under derived.render_only_vs_lvgl. This chart shows the ABSOLUTE ratio; the big chart below indexes every series to its own first observation, which is right for a trend but double-normalises a ratio (a falling line there means the gap shrank, not that vyr passed LVGL).

Every numeric series, indexed to its own first observation

The tables carry levels; this carries change. The series share no unit — instructions per frame are tens of millions, heap is hundreds of thousands of bytes, ns per frame is hundreds, fold share is a fraction — so raw values on one axis would be meaningless, and a second y-axis would invent a correlation the data does not contain. Instead every series is divided by its own first recorded value and multiplied by 100. The axis is therefore dimensionless: 100 is that series’ own first observation, not a share of anything, and 50 means “half what it first was” for every line alike.

64 series on 51 runs. A series needs two observations to be a trend, so the 0 recorded only once are not drawn here — the tables have them. A further 4 cannot be indexed at all, because a first observation of 0 has no ratio to it (qemu-m4 · exact · 2 · fastpath_coverage_pct, qemu-m4 · exact · 3 · fastpath_coverage_pct, qemu-m4 · exact · s · fastpath_coverage_pct, qemu-m4 · exact · z · fastpath_coverage_pct) — also in the tables.

drag on the plot to zoom · double-click to reset

Hover a line to name it: the nearest series lifts, the rest fade, and the readout gives its key, the value the ledger recorded at that run, and its index. A gap is a gap — where a series has no observation at a run the line breaks rather than interpolating, and an observation with no neighbour is drawn as a single point. Series that never moved sit exactly on the 100 rule; they are drawn faintly because stability is evidence but it should not drown the lines that moved. Every value plotted here is also a row in the tables below.

The series are grouped by what they measure — one unit and one meaning per group. Tick a group to show or hide all of its lines at once (that is what rescales the chart); expand a group to reach the individual tier / opt-level lines inside it. This changes only the chart; the tables below always hold every value.

Matrix cells

One row per measurement cell — platform × tier × opt-level × run — with every field the ledger carries for it, including the provenance of each figure and the written reason behind every null.

Click a column header to sort it; click again to reverse. Numeric columns sort numerically. Drag a header to reorder, and use its ⋮ menu to hide columns. A dotted-underlined value carries the reason the ledger recorded for it — hover to read it.

Every other recorded value

The host resolution ladder, anim and cross-ISA runs, bench medians, static size, stock-QEMU M4 quantities, real silicon, the projections the ledger derives and the matrix's own metadata. These sections have different shapes, so each recorded value is its own row: filter section or sort path to get a series back.

Click a column header to sort it; click again to reverse. Numeric columns sort numerically. Drag a header to reorder, and use its ⋮ menu to hide columns. A dotted-underlined value carries the reason the ledger recorded for it — hover to read it.

Runs

One row per ledger entry, including the schema note and any commit that could not be measured. has … is 1 where the run recorded that section — rows are sparse because a run records what it measured and nothing else.

Click a column header to sort it; click again to reverse. Numeric columns sort numerically. Drag a header to reorder, and use its ⋮ menu to hide columns. A dotted-underlined value carries the reason the ledger recorded for it — hover to read it.
